Mass
măs
n. (the Roman rite of the eucharist, held to be a propitiatory sacrifice)
Late Latin missa, from the dismissal formula Ite, missa est at the close of the service; the name of the dismissal became the name of the rite.

Biblical Definition

The mass is the Roman service of the eucharist, defined at Trent as a true and propitiatory sacrifice offered by a priest for the living and the dead. Hebrews sets the whole weight of its argument against exactly that: “every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (Heb 10:11), “but this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12), “for by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). He “needeth not daily… to offer up sacrifice… for this he did once, when he offered up himself” (Heb 7:27).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines mass as the service of the Romish church at the celebration of the eucharist; and, as a distinct word, a lump, a body of matter, a great quantity.

expand to see more

MASS, n. In the Roman Catholic church, the office or prayers used at the celebration of the eucharist; the consecration of the bread and wine.

MASS, n. A lump; a body of matter concreted, collected or formed into a lump.

2. A large quantity; a collective body.

3. Bulk; magnitude.

Key Scripture

Heb 10:11 — "And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins:"

Heb 10:12 — "But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;"

Heb 10:14 — "For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."

Heb 7:27 — "Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself."

Heb 9:26 — "For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself."

1Co 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."

Modern Corruption

A sacrifice is offered again, and Hebrews proves the sacrifice finished by the fact that the Priest sat down.

expand to see more

The argument of Hebrews 10 turns on a posture. Every priest under the law standeth daily, offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins; this Man, having offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down. A seated priest is a finished sacrifice, and the writer draws the conclusion himself two verses later: “Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin” (Heb 10:18). A rite that offers again, however reverently, denies in its action the thing it means to honour, and the calendar of its repetition is the confession that it has not finished.

The Reformed objection is not to the Supper's solemnity or to calling it a sacrifice of praise; the Confession itself calls the ordinance a memorial and a spiritual feeding, and treats it with more seriousness than most of its modern heirs. The objection is to propitiation. The Supper shews the Lord's death till he come (1Co 11:26) — it proclaims a death already died, and it does not re-present it to the Father. Rome's own definition at Trent, that the sacrifice of the mass is truly propitiatory and that by it the anger of God is appeased, is the sentence Hebrews was written to make impossible.

There is a Protestant corruption of the same doctrine, which is to make the Supper nothing at all — a monthly formality with no presence, no feeding, and no fear. The Confession's word is that worthy receivers do really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified. Between a sacrifice repeated and a symbol emptied, the Reformed have held a third thing: a real feeding on a finished work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek thusia (G2378), a sacrifice; prosphora (G4376), an offering; hapax (G530) and ephapax (G2178), once, once for all.

expand to see more

Greek thusia (G2378) — sacrifice; Hebrews 10:11–12, 10:26, 13:15, the sacrifice of praise.

Greek prosphora (G4376) — offering; Hebrews 10:10, 10:14, 10:18.

Greek ephapax (G2178) — once for all; Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10, Romans 6:10.

Usage

"“This man… sat down on the right hand of God” — a seated priest is a finished sacrifice."

"“Where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin” — the writer's own conclusion."

"“Ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” — proclaimed, not re-presented."
